title: List, Set and Map Interfaces
learningObjectives: Declare collection variables using List, Set and Map interfaces
Choose concrete implementations that satisfy required behavior
Explain how lists and sets differ in duplicate handling

Reduce implementation coupling by accepting interface parameters

understand.concept: Use List, Set or Map when callers need the interface contract. ArrayList, HashSet and HashMap differ in ordering, duplicate handling and lookup behavior.
understand.whyItMatters: List, Set and Map Interfaces helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Program to collection interfaces

Collection interfaces describe the operations callers may rely on without requiring one concrete storage strategy. Use `List<E>` for an ordered sequence with duplicates, `Set<E>` for unique elements, and `Map<K,V>` for key/value associations. Map is separate from the Collection interface hierarchy.

## Declare the contract; construct the implementation

A declaration such as `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` exposes List operations to the rest of the program while constructing an ArrayList. The variable can later refer to another List implementation if that implementation satisfies the same required contract. Declaring the variable as ArrayList unnecessarily couples the code to that class when only List behavior is needed.

## Understand the boundaries

List supports indexed access and duplicate values. Set prevents duplicates according to its implementation's equality or comparison rules. Map has unique keys; putting a value under an existing key replaces the previous mapping. Collection is a broader superinterface for many element collections, but it does not provide Map's key-based operations.

## Interface choice does not promise performance

The interface tells you what operations mean, not that every implementation has the same time complexity or ordering. ArrayList and LinkedList both implement List but have different performance characteristics. HashSet and LinkedHashSet both implement Set but differ in encounter order. HashMap and TreeMap both implement Map but differ in ordering and operation costs.

## Design flexible APIs

Accept an interface when a method needs only that contract, and return the narrowest useful abstraction. Use generics to preserve type safety. Test only behavior guaranteed by the chosen interface; test implementation-specific ordering only when that implementation is deliberately part of the requirement.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<String> names = new java.util.ArrayList<>(); names.add("A"); names.add("B"); System.out.println(names.size()); } }
examples.explanation: The variable is declared as List, so callers rely on the List contract while ArrayList supplies the concrete storage.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Set<String> tags = new java.util.LinkedHashSet<>(); tags.add("java"); tags.add("java"); System.out.println(tags.size()); } }
examples.explanation: LinkedHashSet implements Set: the repeated tag is rejected, so the resulting set contains one element.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<String,Integer> scores = new java.util.HashMap<>(); scores.put("Mira", 90); System.out.println(scores.get("Mira")); } }
examples.explanation: Map associates a student key with a score; get retrieves the value for the exact key.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Collection<Integer> values = java.util.List.of(2,4,6); int total=0; for(int v:values) total+=v; System.out.println(total); } }
examples.explanation: Collection is a superinterface for element collections, allowing enhanced-for traversal without depending on List-specific indexing.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<Integer> values = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of(3,1,2)); java.util.Collections.sort(values); System.out.println(values); } }
examples.explanation: Collections.sort accepts a List and orders its elements in place; the declared List interface is sufficient for this operation.

practise.guidedTask: Declare variables using List, Set and Map interfaces, then assign ArrayList, LinkedHashSet and HashMap implementations. Demonstrate each interface's contract.
practise.independentTask: Refactor a method to accept List<String> instead of ArrayList<String>. Pass two different List implementations without changing the method.
hints: Declare variables and parameters with the narrowest interface that provides the operations your code needs.
Remember Map is not a Collection; its keySet, values and entrySet views expose different parts of its mappings.
Do not infer ordering or time complexity from an interface name; inspect the concrete implementation contract.
practise.challenge: Write a short API design note identifying which behaviors belong to interfaces and which depend on the concrete implementation.

questions.prompt: Which declaration reduces coupling to a specific list implementation?
questions.explanation: Declaring the variable as List exposes the interface contract while allowing the implementation to be replaced by another List implementation.

questions.prompt: Which interface permits duplicate elements and positional access?
questions.explanation: List permits duplicates and provides positional operations such as get(index).
Set represents unique elements; it does not provide List-style positional access.
Map models key/value mappings and is not a subtype of Collection.

options: The implementation can change while callers rely on the same contract
questions.answer: The implementation can change while callers rely on the same contract
questions.explanation: Programming to an interface reduces coupling, but does not guarantee constant-time operations or prevent exceptions.
